input: Given /data/team_a.txt and /data/team_b.txt containing member names (one per line, already sorted), use the comm command to find: 1) Members only in Team A (print under 'Only Team A:'). 2) Members only in Team B (print under 'Only Team B:'). 3) Members in both teams (print under 'Both teams:'). Print the count of each group.

transcript.final_response:
Results using `comm` on the two sorted files:

**How it works:** `comm file1 file2` outputs 3 columns: lines only in file1 (col 1), lines only in file2 (col 2), and lines in both (col 3). The flags `-1`, `-2`, `-3` suppress each respective column:

- `comm -23` → only in Team A (suppress cols 2 and 3)
- `comm -13` → only in Team B (suppress cols 1 and 3)
- `comm -12` → in both teams (suppress cols 1 and 2)

**Output:**

```
Only Team A:
alice
dave
eve
Count: 3

Only Team B:
frank
grace
Count: 2

Both teams:
bob
carol
Count: 2
```

**Verification:** Team A has 5 members (3 unique + 2 shared ✓) and Team B has 4 members (2 unique + 2 shared ✓).
tool_calls: ls -la /data/team_a.txt /data/team_b.txt && echo "--- team_a.txt ---" && cat /data/team_a.txt && echo "--- team_b.txt ---" && cat /data/team_b.txt

only_a=$(comm -23 /data/team_a.txt /data/team_b.txt)
only_b=$(comm -13 /data/team_a.txt /data/team_b.txt)
both=$(comm -12 /data/team_a.txt /data/team_b.txt)

count_a=$(printf '%s\n' "$only_a" | grep -c .)
count_b=$(printf '%s\n' "$only_b" | grep -c .)
count_both=$(printf '%s\n' "$both" | grep -c .)

echo "Only Team A:"
printf '%s\n' "$only_a"
echo "Count: $count_a"
echo
echo "Only Team B:"
printf '%s\n' "$only_b"
echo "Count: $count_b"
echo
echo "Both teams:"
printf '%s\n' "$both"
echo "Count: $count_both"
